fetched_contents.text: Cystic and Cystic-Appearing Lesions of the Mandible: Review Objective Cystic and cystic-appearing lesions of the mandible are commonly noted on head and neck imaging and present a diagnostic dilemma for the radiologist. This article aims to help outline the differential diagnosis for cystic mandibular lesions, outline the key imaging features, and suggest recommendations for further imaging and/or intervention when required. Conclusion After completing this article, the reader should have an improved ability to characterize cystic and cystic-appearing lesions of the mandible. By definition, a cyst is an epithelium-lined cavity that contains fluid or semisolid material. Pathologic analysis of the epithelial lining and contents and clinical and radiographic findings are generally required to achieve a definitive diagnosis [1]. Clinically, cysts in the mandible can present as functional disturbances caused by bone remodeling and weakening. Furthermore, cysts can present after a secondary infection. Cysts occurring in the mandible appear radiographically as either unilocular or multilocular lucencies that vary in size and definition. Displaced or resorbed tooth roots, displaced mandibular canal and expansion, and uneruption of the tooth are often seen. The cyst's spatial relationship to the tooth on imaging is an important diagnostic feature [1]. Accurate radiographic identification of cystic-appearing benign and malignant tumors is essential for appropriate clinical workup and management. Based on the cell of origin, cystic lesions in the mandible are subdivided into odontogenic (Appendix 1) and nonodontogenic (Appendix 2) lesions. Odontogenic cysts arise from tooth derivatives, and they are frequently divided into inflammatory and developmental types. Further subdivision can be achieved with histologic analysis of the epithelial lining and with imaging to determine whether calcifications are present and in correlation with clinical findings; occasionally the pathogenesis is unclear [1]. The World Health Organization classification published in 2005 is widely accepted [2]. This classification defines cysts (odontogenic and nonodontogenic cysts) and tumors (benign and malignant types) and further subdivides the lesions on the basis of odontogenic tissue type [2]. The majority of these lesions may initially be identified by the patient's dentist on either physical examination or routine dental radiographs. Further, cystic lesions are often identified as incidental lesions by the radiologist on imaging performed for different reasons. Collaborative interaction between the dentist, oral surgeon, and radiologist is essential for the appropriate evaluation, imaging, and treatment of cystic and cysticappearing lesions of the mandible (Tables 1 and 2). Odontogenic Lesions Humans have 20 primary and 32 permanent teeth. Each tooth develops from ectoderm and mesenchyme. The ectoderm develops into the enamel, whereas the mesenchymal cells form the dentin, cementum, periodontal ligament, and pulp contents [3, 4]. The dental lamina, a thickening of the oral epithelium, invaginates into the mesenchyme and the surrounding cells condense to form the tooth buds or tooth germs [3]. As the tooth bud grows, it develops into a cap shape with mesenchymal invagination, which forms the dental papilla [4]. The dental papilla forms both the dental pulp (the soft tissue in the root chamber of the tooth that contains nerves, vessels, and connective tissue) and odontoblasts, which form the dentin of the tooth. The ectoderm forms the enamel organ, which includes the outer enamel epithelium, the stellate reticulum, and the inner enamel epithelium. The inner enamel epithelium elongates into ameloblasts, which form the enamel of the tooth [4]. Odontogenic Cysts Cysts commonly occur in the mandible and appear as unilocular or multilocular radiolucencies on dental radiographs. Cystic lesions within the mandible can cause bony remodeling that can weaken the bone, leading to functional changes and predisposing the patient to infection and pathologic fracture [1]. The relationship of the cyst to adjacent structures is important, which includes features such as unerupted teeth, tooth displacement, root resorption, and canal displacement. Although many odontogenic cysts are developmental in origin, the most common type of odontogenic cyst, the periapical cyst, is acquired [5]. Periapical (radicular) cysts—The periapical (radicular) cyst is the most common type of odontogenic cyst. These lesions have a slight male predominance and peak incidence between the ages of 30 and 50 years [5]. Periapical cysts generally originate after trauma or dental caries. Dental caries cause inflammation of the pulp cavity leading to pulp necrosis [6]. The infection then spreads to the tooth apex of the root causing periapical periodontitis, which leads to either an acute abscess or a chronic granuloma. Persistent chronic infection can lead to formation of a periapical cyst [1]. Treatment options include tooth extraction, endodontic therapy, and apical surgery. If the periapical cyst persists after surgical extraction of the associated tooth, it is referred to as a “residual cyst” [5]. A periapical cyst presents as a well-circumscribed corticated radiolucency at the apex of the nonvital tooth. Cortical expansion may be seen with large lesions (Figs. 1 and 2). Periapical cysts can cause root resorption of the affected tooth and can displace adjacent structures including adjacent teeth and the mandibular canal. MRI of periapical cysts shows high T2 (due to high fluid content) and variable T1 signal intensity (Fig. 3). Contrast-enhanced MR images show an enhancing cystic wall consistent with inflammation [1]. Stoneman, DDS, FRCD(C) ABSTRACT The mandibular buccal bifurcation cyst (BBC) was first described by Stoneman and Worth in 1983. It is a lesion with a specific location, classically the buccal surface of the mandibular first molar and less frequently the mandibular second molar. There have been numerous reports in the literature describing the BBC and its treatment. Treatment advocated thus far includes extraction of the involved first molar, marsupialization and enucleation of the cyst. In their most recent article, Pompura, S ndor and Stoneman reported on the successful treatment of 44 cysts with enucleation without tooth extraction. This article will describe the diagnostic features of the BBC and present three cases with a total of five cysts, which were treated non-surgically and ultimately resolved. The authors, therefore, propose that a more conservative non-surgical approach to these lesions may be considered. MeSH Key Words:mandibular diseases/pathology; molar; child; periodontal cyst/pathology. J Can Dent Assoc 1998; 64:712-6 This article has been peer reviewed. [ Introduction | Cases | Discussion] Introduction The buccal bifurcation cyst (BBC) is an uncommon lesion associated with the permanent mandibular first or second molar in children. Usually it is identified just prior to eruption. Stoneman and Worth in 1983 were the first to describe the lesion and report its radiographic and clinical features.1 They named the lesion mandibular infected buccal cyst. Similar lesions have been described in the literature under a variety of names. They include the circumferential dentigerous cyst,2 the inflammatory paradental cyst,3 and the inflammatory collateral dental cyst.4 The World Health Organization5 describes this lesion under the name "paradental cyst." Neville, Damm and Allen et al. state that this latter name should be avoided because it is non-specific.6 Pompura, S ndor and Stoneman7 argue for the term BBC, because the lesion is site- and age- specific. It has a constant relationship to the mandibular first molar's buccal bifurcation (Table I). Table I Clinical Features of the Buccal Bifurcation Cyst 1. Most common in the 6- to 11-year-old age group. 2. Usually associated with the mandibular first molar, occasionally the mandibular second molar. 3. The associated tooth has an altered eruption pattern with buccal tilting of the crown. 4. The associated tooth is vital. 5. Deep periodontal pockets on the buccal aspect of the tooth. 6. +/- swelling. 7. +/- pain or tenderness. 8. +/- infection. The radiographic presentation of the BBC may be subtle and easily overlooked unless the lesion is large or symptomatic. If a BBC is suspected, a panoramic or periapical radiograph should be taken as well as an occlusal film (Fig. 1).1 The BBC's distinct radiographic features are listed in Table II. Table II Radiographic Features of the Buccal Bifurcation Cyst 1. Fine radiopaque concave line as lower limit, producing a U-shaped radiolucent lesion that appears superimposed over the roots. 2. Intact periodontal ligament space and lamina dura. 3. Increased prominence of lingual cusps due to tilting. 4. Apices tilted toward lingual cortex. 5. Intact inferior border of mandible. 6. +/- periosteal reaction on buccal surface. 7. +/- bony expansion, thinning and associated swelling of the buccal cortex. 8. +/- displacement of adjacent unerupted teeth (see Fig. 2a). The histology of this lesion is non-specific and reveals non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, areas of epithelial hyperplasia and an inflammatory infiltrate in the connective tissue wall. Bacteriology reports have shown a mixed flora.7-9 The differential diagnosis of this lesion includes eosinophilic granuloma, lateral periodontal cyst, traumatic bone cyst and periostitis ossificans. Usually, the clinical and radiographic features distinguish the BBC from other conditions.8 Treatment of the BBC has evolved over time. The low incidence of this lesion makes randomized controlled trials impractical. Stoneman and Worth report successful treatment through tooth extraction and curettage of the lesion, as well as with endodontic treatment of the tooth and curettage of the lesion.1 Enucleation and extraction are reported by Trask, Sheller and Morton10 and more recently by Martinez-Conde, Aguirre and Pindborg.11 Stanback reports treatment via marsupialization.12 Enucleation alone is reported by several authors.8,9,13,14 Pompura, S ndor and Stoneman7 recently report the successful treatment of 44 BBCs with enucleation alone (without tooth extraction). He was asymptomatic, but on intraoral examination buccal tilting of the associated teeth and deep buccal periodontal pockets were noted. Mild bilateral swelling was noted extraorally. The lesions were pointed out to the patient and his mother, who were advised to see an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for management. The family moved away for a year and never sought treatment. At a follow-up visit 15 months later, the lesions showed definite signs of radiographic resolution. Six months after this initial follow-up, there was no clinical or radiographic evidence of the cysts at all (Figs. 2a-2f). Case 2 A 9-year-old male had BBCs associated with teeth 3.6 and 4.6. ## Mini-report: imaging and differential diagnosis of Buccal Bifurcation Cyst

The imaging appearance of a buccal bifurcation cyst is best understood as a cystic lesion that is often subtle or easily overlooked on routine radiographs. The authoritative review says that the diagnosis is made based solely on clinical and radiographic features and that BBCs are typically unilateral [N2-R2]. The AJR review further explains that cystic lesions in the mandible appear as unilocular or multilocular lucencies on dental radiographs and that the relationship of the cyst to adjacent structures is important, including features such as unerupted teeth, tooth displacement, root resorption, and canal displacement [N2-F2].

### Radiographic appearance and distinguishing features
The AJR review emphasizes that the spatial relationship of the lesion to the tooth is an important diagnostic feature [N2-F2]. For BBCs specifically, the review notes that the cyst is often subtle and may be overlooked unless large or symptomatic [N2-R2]. It also describes the broader context of mandibular cystic lesions, which can present as unilocular or multilocular radiolucencies with varying size and definition, and that displaced or resorbed tooth roots, displaced mandibular canal, and unerupted teeth are often seen [N2-F2]. This helps distinguish BBCs from other cysts by their association with eruption-related morphology.

The case report and literature review provide more specific features of BBC radiographic appearance. It states that the BBC’s distinct radiographic features include a fine radiopaque concave line as the lower limit, producing a U-shaped radiolucent lesion superimposed over the roots, intact periodontal ligament space and lamina dura, increased prominence of lingual cusps due to tilting, apices tilted toward the lingual cortex, intact inferior border of the mandible, and possible periosteal reaction, bony expansion, thinning, and associated swelling of the buccal cortex [N5-F3]. These features are important because they help distinguish BBC from other radiolucencies that may appear similar on routine imaging.

### Differential diagnoses commonly confused with BBC
Several sources explicitly list differential diagnoses. The 2019 bilateral mandibular BBC case report mentions dentigerous cyst, lateral radicular cyst, and periodontal pocket as possible differentials [N2-R1]. The AJR review lists cystic and cystic-appearing lesions and notes that accurate radiographic identification is essential because these lesions may be benign or malignant [N2-F2]. The authoritative review also includes eosinophilic granuloma, lateral periodontal cyst, traumatic bone cyst, and periostitis ossificans in the differential diagnosis [N2-R3]. Another source expands this list to include circumferential dentigerous cyst, inflammatory paradental cyst, inflammatory collateral dental cyst, and, by some authors, paradental cyst more generally [N5-F3]. The AJR review also notes that non-odontogenic lesions should be considered, which broadens the differential beyond purely dental etiologies [N2-F2].

### Role of CT/MRI in confirming or excluding the diagnosis
The evidence is clearer for MRI than for CT. The AJR review states that MRI of periapical cysts shows high T2 signal due to high fluid content and variable T1 signal intensity, while contrast-enhanced MR images show an enhancing cystic wall consistent with inflammation [N2-F2]. This suggests that MRI can help characterize the cyst’s content and wall reaction, which is useful for distinguishing BBC from other inflammatory or cystic lesions. The case report and literature review do not provide specific CT findings, but the broader AJR review indicates that CT is useful for evaluating bony expansion, displacement, and relationship to adjacent structures [N2-F2]. In practice, CT may be more useful for assessing bony anatomy, whereas MRI is better for soft-tissue and fluid characterization.

### When imaging suggests a different entity than a simple cyst
The AJR review explicitly states that accurate radiographic identification of cystic-appearing benign and malignant tumors is essential for appropriate clinical workup and management [N2-F2]. It also notes that the diagnosis is not made solely on imaging and that pathologic analysis of epithelial lining and contents, along with clinical and radiographic findings, are generally required for a definitive diagnosis [N2-F2]. The BBC review similarly emphasizes that the clinical and radiographic features usually distinguish the lesion from other conditions [N5-F3]. Therefore, if imaging shows features inconsistent with a simple unilocular cyst—such as aggressive bony expansion, atypical soft-tissue enhancement, or evidence of malignancy—the diagnosis should not be assumed and further imaging or biopsy should be considered [N2-F2].

Overall, BBC imaging is best interpreted in context: it often presents as a subtle, cyst-like radiolucency near a developing or erupting molar, with specific radiographic signs such as a U-shaped lesion, intact lamina dura, and buccal tilting, and it is best distinguished from other cysts, granulomas, and inflammatory lesions by a combination of imaging and clinical findings [N2-R2][N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Mini-report: management and treatment decision-making

Management of BBC is generally conservative, with a preference for enucleation or curettage without extraction of the associated tooth. The evidence shows that most current literature supports simple enucleation and curettage of the cyst without extraction of the involved tooth as the treatment of choice [N4-R1]. A similar source states that conservative treatment such as curettage or enucleation without extraction of the associated tooth was preferred [N4-R2]. Another source says that surgical management by cyst enucleation without extraction of the involved tooth seems to be the treatment of choice [N4-R4]. These statements are consistent with the broader authoritative review, which notes that treatment has evolved over time and that non-surgical approaches, including enucleation and even more conservative methods, are being considered [N5-F3].

### Indications for observation vs intervention
The evidence suggests that observation is appropriate when the lesion is small, asymptomatic, or not clinically significant. The authoritative review notes that BBC is often asymptomatic but can present with infection, drainage of pus, and pain [N5-F3]. It also reports a case in which asymptomatic bilateral cystic lesions resolved after follow-up without active treatment [N5-F3]. This supports the idea that observation can be reasonable in low-risk, asymptomatic cases. However, intervention is indicated when the lesion is symptomatic, enlarging, or associated with infection, pus, or pain [N5-F3]. The AJR review similarly notes that cysts can present after secondary infection, which implies that infection may justify more active management [N2-F2].

### Surgical management options and timing
The main surgical options described are enucleation, curettage, and marsupialization. The authoritative review states that treatment advocated thus far includes extraction of the involved first molar, marsupialization, and enucleation of the cyst [N5-F3]. It also notes that enucleation alone is reported by several authors and that a recent series reported successful treatment of 44 BBCs with enucleation without tooth extraction [N5-F3]. A separate source says that most current literature supports simple enucleation and curettage without extraction of the involved tooth [N4-R1]. Another source explicitly says that enucleation or even more conservative methods should be used, and that the affected teeth should be preserved if possible [N4-R5]. Timing is generally related to the clinical picture: when the lesion is large, symptomatic, or showing signs of infection, intervention is preferred. The review also reports a case in which a cyst enlarged and required surgical treatment during follow-up, whereas the other cyst regressed without treatment [N5-F3]. This suggests that timing is often guided by clinical progression rather than a fixed schedule.

### Follow-up and recurrence considerations
Follow-up is an important part of management. The authoritative review reports a case in which lesions showed definite signs of radiographic resolution after 15 months of follow-up, and the cysts had disappeared entirely after six months [N5-F3]. This indicates that close follow-up can be useful to monitor resolution and recurrence. The AJR review notes that cystic lesions can cause bony remodeling and may predispose to infection and pathologic fracture, which implies that follow-up should include monitoring for structural changes and infection [N2-F2]. Recurrence is a concern, but the evidence does not provide a precise recurrence rate. Instead, it emphasizes that treatment and follow-up should be individualized and that non-surgical approaches are being increasingly considered [N5-F3].

### Impact of associated teeth on treatment planning
The associated tooth is central to treatment planning. The authoritative review states that the associated tooth has an altered eruption pattern with buccal tilting of the crown and that the tooth is typically vital [N5-F3]. It also notes that deep periodontal pockets, swelling, and pain can be present [N5-F3]. These features mean that treatment should preserve the associated tooth where possible, because the tooth is usually vital and the cyst is closely related to eruption [N5-F3]. The evidence also supports non-extraction approaches, which is important because extraction may be unnecessary and may carry its own risks [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The AJR review further highlights that the cyst’s spatial relationship to the tooth is an important diagnostic feature, reinforcing that treatment must take the tooth and eruption pattern into account [N2-F2].

In summary, management of BBC is usually conservative, with enucleation or curettage preferred over extraction, and timing depends on symptoms, infection, and clinical progression. Observation is reasonable for asymptomatic cases, while intervention is indicated when the lesion is active or infected. Follow-up is important to monitor resolution and recurrence, and treatment planning should preserve the associated tooth where possible [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N5-F3].

## Mini-report: typical clinical features of Buccal Bifurcation Cyst in molars

BBC is a rare, inflammatory odontogenic cyst typically affecting the buccal region of the first or second mandibular molars in children [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F3]. It is most commonly associated with the mandibular first molar, with less frequent involvement of the mandibular second molar [N1-R2][N5-F3]. The authoritative review states that BBC is usually identified just prior to eruption and that it is uncommonly associated with the second molar [N5-F3]. A separate source reports that it occurs in children between 4 and 14 years and predominantly affects the mandibular first molar [N1-F1]. This age distribution is important because it indicates that BBC is a pediatric or early adolescent condition rather than a late adult one.

### Presence of eruption cyst or associated tooth signs
The most consistent associated tooth signs are altered eruption pattern, buccal tilting of the crown, and deep periodontal pockets [N5-F3]. The authoritative review also states that the associated tooth is vital [N5-F3]. The evidence repeatedly links BBC to eruption-related morphology: it is often described as occurring just prior to eruption and as being associated with partial tooth eruption, crown tilting, and deep buccal periodontal pockets [N1-R5][N5-F3]. The case report and literature review describe a partial eruption of the right permanent mandibular first molar with drainage of purulent material and clinical absence of the left mandibular first molar [N1-F1]. This suggests that eruption-related trauma or the process of eruption can be central to the clinical picture.

### Asymptomatic vs symptomatic presentation and symptoms
BBC is often asymptomatic, but it can be symptomatic. The authoritative review notes that BBC is often asymptomatic but infection, with drainage of pus, and pain can be present [N5-F3]. The case report and literature review describe a 9-year-old boy with an extraoral soft tissue painful swelling and purulent drainage [N1-F1]. This indicates that BBC can present with both asymptomatic and symptomatic features, with infection being a common source of symptoms. The AJR review also notes that cysts can present after secondary infection, which supports the idea that symptomatic presentation is often infection-related [N2-F2].

### Associated clinical findings such as swelling or mucosal changes
Swelling is a common clinical finding. The authoritative review reports that mild bilateral swelling may be noted extraorally [N5-F3]. It also notes that buccal bone expansion covered by normal mucosa may be observed adjacent to the involved molars [N1-F1]. The AJR review states that cysts can cause bony remodeling, weakening, and predispose to infection and pathologic fracture, which implies that swelling may be part of a broader inflammatory or structural response [N2-F2]. The case report also describes a painful extraoral swelling and drainage of purulent material, indicating that mucosal changes such as drainage and inflammation may accompany the swelling [N1-F1].

### Overall clinical picture
The clinical picture of BBC in molars is therefore best summarized as a rare, inflammatory, eruption-associated cyst that typically occurs in the buccal region of the mandibular first or second molar, especially in children just before eruption [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F3][N1-F1]. It is often asymptomatic but can be associated with swelling, pain, infection, and purulent drainage. The associated tooth commonly shows altered eruption, buccal tilting, and deep periodontal pockets, and the lesion is often closely related to eruption-related trauma or morphologic changes [N5-F3][N1-R5]. These features make BBC distinct from other cystic lesions in the mandible and emphasize its connection to the eruption process [N5-F3][N1-F1].

## Mini-report: eruption-related pathogenesis and associated tooth effects

The evidence points to eruption or eruption-related trauma as a central mechanism in BBC formation. The authoritative review states that the etiology remains uncertain, but it is postulated that the tooth breaks the oral mucosa during eruption, causing inflammation and a localized response [N3-R1]. It also notes that different theories have been proposed, including the idea that as the cusps penetrate the oral epithelium, a localized area is created that may lead to the lesion [N3-R3]. Another source adds that one theory is that tilting of the molar as it erupts creates a deep periodontal pocket in the area of the perforated epithelium, which causes the cyst to form [N3-R5]. These mechanisms suggest that eruption-related trauma, epithelial disruption, and subsequent inflammation are important in pathogenesis.

### Relationship between enamel projections, ridges, and the buccal bifurcation
The evidence also links enamel projections and ridges to the buccal bifurcation. One source states that the cysts are usually associated with enamel projections or ridges extending into the buccal bifurcation of the dental roots [N3-R2]. Another source expands this by saying that the lesion is often associated with the buccal bifurcation region and that the buccal bifurcation is a key anatomical site [N6-R5]. This relationship is important because it explains why BBC is often located in the buccal bifurcation area of molars and how developmental anomalies or morphologic features of the tooth can contribute to cyst formation [N3-R2][N6-R5].

### Clinical manifestations linked to the erupting tooth or adjacent teeth
Clinical manifestations are closely linked to the erupting tooth and adjacent teeth. The authoritative review lists altered eruption pattern, buccal tilting of the crown, and deep periodontal pockets as key associated features [N5-F3]. The AJR review notes that cystic lesions can cause bony remodeling and displacement of adjacent structures, including adjacent teeth and the mandibular canal [N2-F2]. The case report describes partial eruption of the right permanent mandibular first molar, buccal tilting, and purulent drainage, with adjacent structures affected [N1-F1]. These findings indicate that BBC is not confined to the tooth itself; it can affect eruption, periodontal tissues, and adjacent bony structures.

### Timing of presentation relative to eruption
BBC typically presents just prior to eruption. The authoritative review says it is usually identified just prior to eruption [N5-F3]. The case report in the literature review also describes a 9-year-old boy with a chief complaint of abrupt asymmetric enlargement of the face and partial eruption of the right permanent mandibular first molar [N1-F1]. This timing is important because it suggests that BBC is an eruption-related lesion that emerges as the tooth erupts or is about to erupt, rather than being unrelated to the eruption process [N5-F3][N1-F1].

### Overall eruption-related pathogenesis
Taken together, the evidence supports an eruption-related pathogenesis in which trauma or disruption during eruption creates an epithelial defect, which then becomes lined with epithelium and filled with fluid or inflammatory material [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The presence of enamel projections, ridges, or developmental anomalies in the buccal bifurcation region appears to predispose the area to cyst formation [N3-R2]. Clinically, this manifests as altered eruption, buccal tilting, deep periodontal pockets, and sometimes infection, swelling, and drainage [N5-F3][N1-F1]. The timing of presentation is usually just before eruption, reinforcing the idea that eruption is not merely a backdrop but a central part of the lesion’s origin and clinical expression [N5-F3][N1-F1].

The authoritative review states that BBC is often asymptomatic but infection, with **drainage of pus** and **pain**, can be present [N5-F3]. A case report describes a 9-year-old boy with an **extraoral soft tissue painful swelling** and **purulent drainage** [N1-F1]. This pattern suggests that the lesion can present in two main ways: one where it is silent or barely noticeable, and another where it becomes active, infected, or painful. The AJR review also notes that cysts can present after **secondary infection**, supporting the idea that symptomatic presentation is often infection-related [N2-F2].

### 4) Associated clinical findings such as swelling or mucosal changes

Swelling is a common clinical finding. The authoritative review reports that **mild bilateral swelling** may be noted extraorally [N5-F3]. It also notes that **buccal bone expansion** covered by **normal mucosa** may be observed adjacent to the involved molars [N1-F1]. The AJR review explains that cysts can cause **bony remodeling**, weaken bone, and predispose to infection and pathologic fracture, which implies that swelling may be part of a broader inflammatory or structural response [N2-F2]. The case report further describes a painful extraoral swelling and **drainage of purulent material**, indicating that mucosal changes such as **inflammation and drainage** may accompany the swelling [N1-F1].

### 5) Imaging and differential diagnosis

Although this is not a purely clinical report, the imaging context is important for recognizing BBC. The AJR review states that the diagnosis of a buccal bifurcation cyst is made based solely on **clinical and radiographic features**, and that BBCs are typically **unilateral** [N2-R2]. Radiographically, BBCs appear as **unilocular or multilocular lucencies** on dental radiographs, and the relationship of the cyst to adjacent structures is an important diagnostic feature [N2-F2]. Specific BBC features include a **fine radiopaque concave line as the lower limit**, producing a **U-shaped radiolucent lesion** superimposed over the roots, **intact periodontal ligament space and lamina dura**, **increased prominence of lingual cusps** due to tilting, **apices tilted toward the lingual cortex**, **intact inferior border of the mandible**, and **possible periosteal reaction, bony expansion, thinning, and associated swelling of the buccal cortex** [N5-F3]. These imaging features help distinguish BBC from other cystic lesions.

The differential diagnosis includes several odontogenic and non-odontogenic conditions. The 2019 case report lists **dentigerous cyst**, **lateral radicular cyst**, and **periodontal pocket** as possible differentials [N2-R1]. The AJR review notes that accurate radiographic identification of **cystic-appearing benign and malignant tumors** is essential and that pathologic analysis of the epithelial lining and contents, along with clinical and radiographic findings, is generally required for a definitive diagnosis [N2-F2]. The authoritative review also includes **eosinophilic granuloma**, **lateral periodontal cyst**, **traumatic bone cyst**, and **periostitis ossificans** in the differential diagnosis [N2-R3]. Other sources expand the differential to include **circumferential dentigerous cyst**, **inflammatory paradental cyst**, and **inflammatory collateral dental cyst**, with some authors preferring the term **BBC** because it is **site- and age-specific** [N5-F3].

CT and MRI play a complementary role. CT is useful for evaluating **bony expansion**, **displacement**, and the **relationship to adjacent structures**, while MRI shows **high T2 signal** due to high fluid content and **variable T1 signal intensity**, with **contrast-enhanced MR images** showing an **enhancing cystic wall** consistent with inflammation [N2-F2]. The AJR review emphasizes that imaging should not be used in isolation, because the diagnosis is not made solely on imaging and requires **clinical and radiographic findings** in combination with histopathologic analysis if needed [N2-F2]. If imaging suggests a lesion that is not a simple cyst—such as one with **aggressive bony expansion**, **atypical soft-tissue enhancement**, or **evidence of malignancy**—further imaging or biopsy should be considered [N2-F2].

### 6) Pathogenesis and eruption-related effects

The evidence points to **eruption or eruption-related trauma** as a central mechanism in BBC formation. The authoritative review states that the etiology remains uncertain, but it is postulated that the tooth breaks the oral mucosa during eruption, causing inflammation and a localized response [N3-R1]. It also notes that different theories have been proposed, including the idea that as the cusps penetrate the oral epithelium, a localized area is created that may lead to the lesion [N3-R3]. Another source adds that one theory is that **tilting of the molar as it erupts** creates a **deep periodontal pocket** in the area of the perforated epithelium, which causes the cyst to form [N3-R5]. These mechanisms suggest that eruption-related trauma, epithelial disruption, and subsequent inflammation are important in pathogenesis.

Enamel projections and ridges are also important. One source states that the cysts are usually associated with **enamel projections or ridges extending into the buccal bifurcation of the dental roots** [N3-R2]. Another source expands this by saying that the lesion is often associated with the **buccal bifurcation region** [N6-R5]. This relationship is important because it explains why BBC is often located in the buccal bifurcation area of molars and how developmental anomalies or morphologic features of the tooth can contribute to cyst formation [N3-R2][N6-R5].

Clinically, this manifests as **altered eruption**, **buccal tilting of the crown**, and **deep periodontal pockets** [N5-F3]. The AJR review notes that cystic lesions can cause **bony remodeling** and **displacement of adjacent structures**, including adjacent teeth and the **mandibular canal** [N2-F2]. The case report describes **partial eruption** of the right permanent mandibular first molar, **buccal tilting**, and **purulent drainage**, with adjacent structures affected [N1-F1]. These findings indicate that BBC is not confined to the tooth itself; it can affect eruption, periodontal tissues, and adjacent bony structures.

### 7) Timing of presentation relative to eruption

BBC typically presents **just prior to eruption**. The authoritative review states that BBC is usually identified just prior to eruption [N5-F3]. The case report in the literature review also describes a 9-year-old boy with a chief complaint of **abrupt asymmetric enlargement of the face** and **partial eruption** of the right permanent mandibular first molar [N1-F1]. This timing is important because it suggests that BBC is an **eruption-related lesion** that emerges as the tooth erupts or is about to erupt, rather than being unrelated to the eruption process [N5-F3][N1-F1].

### 8) Overall clinical picture

In summary, the typical clinical features of BBC in molars are:

- **Rare, inflammatory, odontogenic cyst** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F3]
- **Usually affects the mandibular first molar**, with **less frequent involvement of the mandibular second molar** [N1-R2][N5-F3]
- **Predominantly seen in children between 4 and 14 years** [N1-F1]
- **Often asymptomatic**, but can be **symptomatic** with **infection**, **pain**, and **purulent drainage** [N5-F3][N1-F1]
- **Commonly associated with altered eruption**, **buccal tilting of the crown**, and **deep periodontal pockets** [N5-F3]
- **May show swelling**, **buccal bone expansion**, and **mucosal changes** [N5-F3][N1-F1]
- **Imaging typically shows a subtle cystic lesion** with **U-shaped radiolucent appearance**, **intact lamina dura**, and **buccal tilting features** [N5-F3][N2-F2]
- **Differential diagnosis** includes **dentigerous cyst**, **lateral radicular cyst**, **periodontal pocket**, **eosinophilic granuloma**, **lateral periodontal cyst**, **traumatic bone cyst**, and **periostitis ossificans** [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R2][N5-F3]
- **Etiology is uncertain**, but **eruption-related trauma**, **epithelial disruption**, and **developmental anomalies in the buccal bifurcation region** are important [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N3-R2][N6-R5]
- **Presentation is usually just prior to eruption**, reinforcing the eruption-related nature of the lesion [N5-F3][N1-F1]

This makes BBC a distinct clinical entity that is closely tied to eruption and the buccal bifurcation region. It is often best recognized by its association with the erupting molar, its subtle imaging appearance, and its potential to be asymptomatic or to become symptomatic with infection [N5-F3][N2-F2][N1-F1].

## Mini-report: imaging and differential diagnosis of Buccal Bifurcation Cyst

The imaging appearance of a buccal bifurcation cyst is best understood as a cystic lesion that is often subtle or easily overlooked on routine radiographs. The authoritative review says that the diagnosis is made based solely on clinical and radiographic features and that BBCs are typically unilateral [N2-R2]. The AJR review further explains that cystic lesions in the mandible appear as unilocular or multilocular lucencies on dental radiographs and that the relationship of the cyst to adjacent structures is important, including features such as unerupted teeth, tooth displacement, root resorption, and canal displacement [N2-F2].

### Radiographic appearance and distinguishing features
The AJR review emphasizes that the spatial relationship of the lesion to the tooth is an important diagnostic feature [N2-F2]. For BBCs specifically, the review notes that the cyst is often subtle and may be overlooked unless large or symptomatic [N2-R2]. It also describes the broader context of mandibular cystic lesions, which can present as unilocular or multilocular radiolucencies with varying size and definition, and that displaced or resorbed tooth roots, displaced mandibular canal, and unerupted teeth are often seen [N2-F2]. This helps distinguish BBCs from other cysts by their association with eruption-related morphology.

The case report and literature review provide more specific features of BBC radiographic appearance. It states that the BBC’s distinct radiographic features include a fine radiopaque concave line as the lower limit, producing a U-shaped radiolucent lesion superimposed over the roots, intact periodontal ligament space and lamina dura, increased prominence of lingual cusps due to tilting, apices tilted toward the lingual cortex, intact inferior border of the mandible, and possible periosteal reaction, bony expansion, thinning, and associated swelling of the buccal cortex [N5-F3]. These features are important because they help distinguish BBC from other radiolucencies that may appear similar on routine imaging.

### Differential diagnoses commonly confused with BBC
Several sources explicitly list differential diagnoses. The 2019 bilateral mandibular BBC case report mentions dentigerous cyst, lateral radicular cyst, and periodontal pocket as possible differentials [N2-R1]. The AJR review lists cystic and cystic-appearing lesions and notes that accurate radiographic identification is essential because these lesions may be benign or malignant [N2-F2]. The authoritative review also includes eosinophilic granuloma, lateral periodontal cyst, traumatic bone cyst, and periostitis ossificans in the differential diagnosis [N2-R3]. Another source expands this list to include circumferential dentigerous cyst, inflammatory paradental cyst, inflammatory collateral dental cyst, and, by some authors, paradental cyst more generally [N5-F3]. The AJR review also notes that non-odontogenic lesions should be considered, which broadens the differential beyond purely dental etiologies [N2-F2].

### Role of CT/MRI in confirming or excluding the diagnosis
The evidence is clearer for MRI than for CT. The AJR review states that MRI of periapical cysts shows high T2 signal due to high fluid content and variable T1 signal intensity, while contrast-enhanced MR images show an enhancing cystic wall consistent with inflammation [N2-F2]. This suggests that MRI can help characterize the cyst’s content and wall reaction, which is useful for distinguishing BBC from other inflammatory or cystic lesions. The case report and literature review do not provide specific CT findings, but the broader AJR review indicates that CT is useful for evaluating bony expansion, displacement, and relationship to adjacent structures [N2-F2]. In practice, CT may be more useful for assessing bony anatomy, whereas MRI is better for soft-tissue and fluid characterization.

### When imaging suggests a different entity than a simple cyst
The AJR review explicitly states that accurate radiographic identification of cystic-appearing benign and malignant tumors is essential for appropriate clinical workup and management [N2-F2]. It also notes that the diagnosis is not made solely on imaging and that pathologic analysis of epithelial lining and contents, along with clinical and radiographic findings, are generally required for a definitive diagnosis [N2-F2]. The BBC review similarly emphasizes that the clinical and radiographic features usually distinguish the lesion from other conditions [N5-F3]. Therefore, if imaging shows features inconsistent with a simple unilocular cyst—such as aggressive bony expansion, atypical soft-tissue enhancement, or evidence of malignancy—the diagnosis should not be assumed and further imaging or biopsy should be considered [N2-F2].

Overall, BBC imaging is best interpreted in context: it often presents as a subtle, cyst-like radiolucency near a developing or erupting molar, with specific radiographic signs such as a U-shaped lesion, intact lamina dura, and buccal tilting, and it is best distinguished from other cysts, granulomas, and inflammatory lesions by a combination of imaging and clinical findings [N2-R2][N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Mini-report: management and treatment decision-making

Management of BBC is generally conservative, with a preference for enucleation or curettage without extraction of the associated tooth. The evidence shows that most current literature supports simple enucleation and curettage of the cyst without extraction of the involved tooth as the treatment of choice [N4-R1]. A similar source states that conservative treatment such as curettage or enucleation without extraction of the associated tooth was preferred [N4-R2]. Another source says that surgical management by cyst enucleation without extraction of the involved tooth seems to be the treatment of choice [N4-R4]. These statements are consistent with the broader authoritative review, which notes that treatment has evolved over time and that non-surgical approaches, including enucleation and even more conservative methods, are being considered [N5-F3].

### Indications for observation vs intervention
The evidence suggests that observation is appropriate when the lesion is small, asymptomatic, or not clinically significant. The authoritative review notes that BBC is often asymptomatic but can present with infection, drainage of pus, and pain [N5-F3]. It also reports a case in which asymptomatic bilateral cystic lesions resolved after follow-up without active treatment [N5-F3]. This supports the idea that observation can be reasonable in low-risk, asymptomatic cases. However, intervention is indicated when the lesion is symptomatic, enlarging, or associated with infection, pus, or pain [N5-F3]. The AJR review similarly notes that cysts can present after secondary infection, which implies that infection may justify more active management [N2-F2].

### Surgical management options and timing
The main surgical options described are enucleation, curettage, and marsupialization. The authoritative review states that treatment advocated thus far includes extraction of the involved first molar, marsupialization, and enucleation of the cyst [N5-F3]. It also notes that enucleation alone is reported by several authors and that a recent series reported successful treatment of 44 BBCs with enucleation without tooth extraction [N5-F3]. A separate source says that most current literature supports simple enucleation and curettage without extraction of the involved tooth [N4-R1]. Another source explicitly says that enucleation or even more conservative methods should be used, and that the affected teeth should be preserved if possible [N4-R5]. Timing is generally related to the clinical picture: when the lesion is large, symptomatic, or showing signs of infection, intervention is preferred. The review also reports a case in which a cyst enlarged and required surgical treatment during follow-up, whereas the other cyst regressed without treatment [N5-F3]. This suggests that timing is often guided by clinical progression rather than a fixed schedule.

### Follow-up and recurrence considerations
Follow-up is an important part of management. The authoritative review reports a case in which lesions showed definite signs of radiographic resolution after 15 months of follow-up, and the cysts had disappeared entirely after six months [N5-F3]. This indicates that close follow-up can be useful to monitor resolution and recurrence. The AJR review notes that cystic lesions can cause bony remodeling and may predispose to infection and pathologic fracture, which implies that follow-up should include monitoring for structural changes and infection [N2-F2]. Recurrence is a concern, but the evidence does not provide a precise recurrence rate. Instead, it emphasizes that treatment and follow-up should be individualized and that non-surgical approaches are being increasingly considered [N5-F3].

### Impact of associated teeth on treatment planning
The associated tooth is central to treatment planning. The authoritative review states that the associated tooth has an altered eruption pattern with buccal tilting of the crown and that the tooth is typically vital [N5-F3]. It also notes that deep periodontal pockets, swelling, and pain can be present [N5-F3]. These features mean that treatment should preserve the associated tooth where possible, because the tooth is usually vital and the cyst is closely related to eruption [N5-F3]. The evidence also supports non-extraction approaches, which is important because extraction may be unnecessary and may carry its own risks [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The AJR review further highlights that the cyst’s spatial relationship to the tooth is an important diagnostic feature, reinforcing that treatment must take the tooth and eruption pattern into account [N2-F2].

In summary, management of BBC is usually conservative, with enucleation or curettage preferred over extraction, and timing depends on symptoms, infection, and clinical progression. Observation is reasonable for asymptomatic cases, while intervention is indicated when the lesion is active or infected. Follow-up is important to monitor resolution and recurrence, and treatment planning should preserve the associated tooth where possible [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N5-F3].

A separate source reports that it occurs in children between 4 and 14 years and predominantly affects the mandibular first molar [N1-F1]. This age distribution is important because it indicates that BBC is a pediatric or early adolescent condition rather than a late adult one.

### Presence of eruption cyst or associated tooth signs
The most consistent associated tooth signs are altered eruption pattern, buccal tilting of the crown, and deep periodontal pockets [N5-F3]. The authoritative review also states that the associated tooth is vital [N5-F3]. The evidence repeatedly links BBC to eruption-related morphology: it is often described as occurring just prior to eruption and as being associated with partial tooth eruption, crown tilting, and deep buccal periodontal pockets [N1-R5][N5-F3]. The case report and literature review describe a partial eruption of the right permanent mandibular first molar with drainage of purulent material and clinical absence of the left mandibular first molar [N1-F1]. This suggests that eruption-related trauma or the process of eruption can be central to the clinical picture.

### Asymptomatic vs symptomatic presentation and symptoms
BBC is often asymptomatic, but it can be symptomatic. The authoritative review notes that BBC is often asymptomatic but infection, with drainage of pus, and pain can be present [N5-F3]. The case report and literature review describe a 9-year-old boy with an extraoral soft tissue painful swelling and purulent drainage [N1-F1]. This indicates that BBC can present with both asymptomatic and symptomatic features, with infection being a common source of symptoms. The AJR review also notes that cysts can present after secondary infection, which supports the idea that symptomatic presentation is often infection-related [N2-F2].

Swelling is a common clinical finding. The authoritative review reports that mild bilateral swelling may be noted extraorally [N5-F3]. The AJR review states that cysts can cause bony remodeling, weakening, and predispose to infection and pathologic fracture, which implies that swelling may be part of a broader inflammatory or structural response [N2-F2]. The case report also describes a painful extraoral swelling and drainage of purulent material, indicating that mucosal changes such as drainage and inflammation may accompany the swelling [N1-F1].

### Overall clinical picture
The clinical picture of BBC in molars is therefore best summarized as a rare, inflammatory, eruption-associated cyst that typically occurs in the buccal region of the mandibular first or second molar, especially in children just before eruption [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F3][N1-F1]. It is often asymptomatic but can be associated with swelling, pain, infection, and purulent drainage. The associated tooth commonly shows altered eruption, buccal tilting, and deep periodontal pockets, and the lesion is often closely related to eruption-related trauma or morphologic changes [N5-F3][N1-R5]. These features make BBC distinct from other cystic lesions in the mandible and emphasize its connection to the eruption process [N5-F3][N1-F1].
